477.title: Living ashtpadi 10
477.hook: seeing the countless makes our worries smaller
477.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 11, salok: the doer of all
477.howItsDone: Sikhs read the 'kaee kot' stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib, and Japji's lines on countless worlds, as hymns of wonder that put personal troubles in the setting of a vast creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kartaa: the proud and the lost, counted too, and only the Creator knows it. Your line was all in the play. Did you set the gavel down? Today, we live ashtpadi ten. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

It's two in the morning, and a worry has taken over the whole room. An email you shouldn't have sent. A bill. A test result. Lying in bed, it feels like the biggest thing in the universe. Then you get up for water, glance out the window, and there, if the sky is clear, are the stars. More than you can count, and more behind those. The worry doesn't vanish. But it shrinks, a little, to its real size. Astronomers didn't invent that feeling, and neither did poets. Ashtpadi ten knew it too.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING, ONE WORRY.` → `A GLANCE AT THE STARS.` → `THE WORRY FINDS ITS REAL SIZE.`

segments.voice: After counting the seekers and the lost, ashtpadi ten widens out even further. Its drumbeat, kaee kot, many millions, moves from people to worlds. One stanza says: many millions are the sources of life and the regions of the earth. Many millions are the skies and the brahmands. Brahmand is a universe, a whole world-system. Many millions of universes. Guru Nanak said something similar in Japji, which we read last year: worlds below worlds, hundreds of thousands of skies above skies, and people grow tired searching for the limit. The Granth isn't giving an astronomy lesson here. It's giving a sense of scale: vast, uncountable, beyond any edge anyone can find. Now, what does it mean to live this? The outline puts it simply: seeing the countless makes our worries smaller. Not unimportant. Smaller. Your worry is real, and it's yours, and in Sukhmani's picture the Creator of many millions of universes holds it too. But it's not the center of everything. That's the gift of ashtpadi ten. It takes you outside on a clear night and says: look how big this is. Look how much is being held. Now, put your worry down for a moment, and see what size it really is.
screen: `FROM PEOPLE TO WORLDS.` · `BRAHMAND: A WHOLE UNIVERSE.` · `JAPJI: SKIES ABOVE SKIES.` · `NOT UNIMPORTANT, JUST SMALLER.` · then, large: `SMALLER WORRIES.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at the stars. If it's night and you can, step outside or go to a window. If it's daytime, close your eyes and picture the darkest, clearest sky you've ever seen. Let your eyes go from one star to the next. Then think: behind every one, more. Let one worry come into your mind, and place it under that sky. Notice its size now. If you pray, you can hand it over to the One who holds the many millions. The bell holds the time.
Brahmand, a universe, a whole world-system. Many millions of brahmands and skies: seeing the countless gives our worries back their real size.
Your line: smaller worries. Tonight, before bed, look at the sky for one minute, or picture it, and let your biggest worry stand under it. Day four hundred seventy-seven.

478.title: Ashtpadi 11, salok: the doer of all
478.hook: karan kaaran prabh ek hai: He alone is the doer and the cause
478.howItsDone: Sikhs read this salok at the opening of Sukhmani's eleventh ashtpadi, and teachers draw on 'karan kaaran' to describe working wholeheartedly while trusting the outcome to Waheguru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, living ashtpadi ten, brahmand: the stars at two in the morning. Your line was smaller worries. Did you look up? Today, ashtpadi eleven opens, and it names who's behind all those skies. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

Watch a toddler pushing a toy steering wheel in the back seat of a car. He turns it hard left; the car happens to turn left. He shouts with delight. He's sure he did that. He turns it right; the car goes straight. He turns it harder. Still straight. Frustration. The grown-ups laugh, because they can see who's actually driving. Then they go back to gripping wheels of their own: the plan, the career, the children's futures, sure that every turn of the road is theirs. The eleventh salok is a short, gentle word about the real driver.
screen: `A TODDLER'S TOY STEERING WHEEL.` → `SURE HE TURNED THE CAR.` → `WHO'S ACTUALLY DRIVING?`

segments.voice: The salok has two lines. The first: karan kaaran prabh ek hai, doosar naahee koe. God alone is the doer and the cause of causes; there is no other. Karan is doing, the deed. Kaaran is the cause, the reason behind the deed. Karan kaaran: the one who does, and the one who makes things be done, the cause behind every cause. Doosar naahee koe: there's no second. The second line: Nanak is a sacrifice to Him, who is in the water, on the land, and in the sky. Balihaar is the word for giving oneself up in love, being a sacrifice to someone. So the line that could sound like cold philosophy, one cause of everything, ends in love, and in a God found everywhere, water, land and sky. Now, a careful point. Sikh teaching doesn't say our choices don't matter. Japji says plainly that we ourselves sow and we ourselves eat what we sow. Sikhs are asked to work hard, earn honestly and act. What the salok takes away is not the effort. It's the illusion that we're the only ones driving. You can turn your wheel with all your heart. You just stop believing the whole road answers to you. That's the peace the salok points to: doing your part fully, and leaving the outcome with the doer of all.
screen: `KARAN: THE DOING. KAARAN: THE CAUSE.` · `DOOSAR NAAHEE KOE: NO SECOND.` · `IN WATER, LAND AND SKY.` · `YOUR PART, NOT THE WHOLE ROAD.` · then, large: `HE IS THE DOER.`

segments.voice: The practice: let go of one outcome. Think of something you're gripping right now, a result you're waiting on. An interview, a diagnosis, a child's choice, a deal. First, honestly name what your part is, and whether you've done it. Then picture your hands on that toy steering wheel. Feel how tight they are. Breathe out, and loosen them, finger by finger. You're still in the car. You still care where it goes. You're just not pretending you're driving the whole road. If you pray, you can place the outcome with the doer of all. The bell holds the time.
Karan kaaran, the doer and the cause of causes. The salok says God alone is this, found in water, land and sky.
Your line: he is the doer. Today, do your part on one thing as well as you can, and then say the line, and let go of how it turns out. Day four hundred seventy-eight.

479.title: His play
479.hook: all happens within His will and His play
479.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of 'bhaana mannana', accepting God's will, especially in grief or hardship, while still working to change what can be changed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the salok of ashtpadi 11: karan kaaran, the doer and the cause of causes. Your line was he is the doer. Did you loosen your grip on one outcome? Today, the first stanza. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

Rain on the morning of the wedding. A flight canceled. The diagnosis nobody wanted. A baby who arrives three weeks early, on the one day everyone was away. Every life has moments when the plan simply doesn't happen, and nothing you could have done would have changed it. Some people rage. Some go numb. In a Sikh home, an elder may say a short phrase, quietly, sometimes through tears: bhaana mannana. Accept the will. It isn't giving up. It's something harder. The first stanza of ashtpadi eleven helps explain what that phrase is reaching for.
screen: `RAIN ON THE WEDDING DAY.` → `NOTHING YOU COULD HAVE DONE.` → `BHAANA MANNANA: ACCEPT THE WILL.`

segments.voice: The stanza begins: God is able to do, and to have things done. Then: jo tis bhaavai soee hog. Whatever pleases Him, that comes to pass. Bhaavai and bhaana belong to the same family of words: what pleases God, and so, the will. Then the pictures arrive fast. In an instant He sets up and takes down. By His order He holds the earth up with no support beneath it. By His order things are born, and by His order they merge back. High and low, every shade and form, all by His order. And then: He makes and makes, and beholds His own greatness. Nanak, He is pervading all. Read that and you might picture a stern ruler issuing commands. But later in Sukhmani, Guru Arjan uses a gentler word for the whole show: khel, play. God makes His own play, the hymn says, and watches it. One way to picture it: a child building a sandcastle, delighting in it, letting the tide take it, and building again. Put the two together, the will and the play, and you get the heart of bhaana mannana. For Sikhs, accepting the will isn't accepting that someone up there is cruel. It's trusting that even the rain on the wedding day is inside the play, though no one can see the whole stage. And here's the careful part: Sikhs who accept the bhaana still grieve, still fight injustice, still call the doctor. Acceptance is about what you can't change. Tomorrow, the stanzas go one step further.
screen: `JO TIS BHAAVAI: WHATEVER PLEASES HIM.` · `SET UP AND TAKEN DOWN IN AN INSTANT.` · `KHEL: CREATION AS PLAY.` · `ACCEPTANCE, NOT GIVING UP.` · then, large: `HIS WILL.`

segments.voice: The practice: accept one thing you can't change. Find one. Not something you can still work on, but something truly fixed: the weather, a past event, someone else's choice, a loss. Hold it in mind. Notice where you push against it in your body: the jaw, the stomach, the shoulders. Breathe into that place. You don't have to like it. Just let it be what it is, inside the play. If you pray, you can say the two words Sikhs use: bhaana mannana. The bell holds the time.
His play. Jo tis bhaavai soee hog: whatever pleases Him comes to pass, and the whole creation is His play, made and watched by its Maker.
Your line: his will. Today, when something you can't change goes wrong, breathe once, say the line, and then do the next thing you can do. Day four hundred seventy-nine.

480.title: Nothing outside
480.howItsDone: Sikhs understand hukam, the divine order, as encompassing everything, as Japji puts it, and many recall it in frustration or hardship as a way of loosening the ego's demand that things go its way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, His play: whatever pleases Him comes to pass, and bhaana mannana, accepting the will. Your line was his will. Today, one word from that same stanza, the one it kept repeating. Day four hundred eighty.

You're stuck in traffic. Not moving. You're going to be late, and there's nothing you can do. Notice what happens inside: the jaw sets, the fingers drum, a voice in your head starts narrating how unfair this is, as if the traffic were happening outside the world, a mistake, a glitch in how things are supposed to go. Most frustration has that shape. This shouldn't be happening. It's outside the plan. The first stanza of ashtpadi eleven has a single word it repeats, line after line, that answers that feeling. The word is hukam.
screen: `STUCK IN TRAFFIC.` → `THIS SHOULDN'T BE HAPPENING.` → `ONE WORD, LINE AFTER LINE.`

segments.voice: Hukam is the divine order, the command, the way God's will runs through everything. You met it last year in Japji. Yesterday you heard the stanza's pictures: the earth held up with no support, things born and merging back, high and low, every color and form. Today, listen to the one word that carries all of them, opening line after line: hukme, by the order. Guru Nanak said it in Japji, in the plainest possible terms: everyone is within the hukam; no one is outside the hukam. That's today's carry, nothing outside. Here's what that does to the traffic jam. The frustration says: this is outside how things should be. Hukam says: there is no outside. The jam is inside the order. So is the meeting you'll be late for. So, for that matter, is your frustration. That doesn't make it pleasant. It doesn't mean God personally arranged a truck to block your lane to teach you a lesson; Sikh teachers don't usually read hukam as that kind of puzzle. It means the frustrating thing isn't a glitch in the universe. It's part of the same order that holds the earth up. And when nothing is outside, there's nothing to fight against in the way frustration wants to fight. Japji also says that whoever understands the hukam stops saying I, I, I. The ego is the part that insists things should go its way. Nothing outside quietly loosens it.
screen: `HUKAM: THE DIVINE ORDER.` · `HUKME, HUKME: BY THE ORDER.` · `NO ONE IS OUTSIDE THE HUKAM.` · `THE FRUSTRATION IS INSIDE TOO.` · then, large: `NOTHING OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: The practice: breathe through one frustration. Bring up something annoying from today, small is fine: a slow line, a rude message, a broken thing. Feel where it lives in you. Now, breathing in, say silently: this too is inside. Breathing out: nothing outside. Don't try to make the feeling go away. Let it be there, held inside the same order as everything else. Keep breathing that way until the edge softens even a little. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
Nothing outside. Everything is within the hukam, the divine order, even what frustrates us; no one and nothing is outside it.
Your line: this too is inside. Next time you're stuck today, in traffic, a line, a delay, breathe in once and say the line on the way out. Day four hundred eighty.

481.title: Living ashtpadi 11
481.hook: trust and effort together: act, and leave the rest
481.howItsDone: Sikhs hold kirat karni, honest effort and work, together with accepting God's will, and teachers quote Guru Arjan's couplet on udam, effort, as the balance between the two.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nothing outside: the hukam holds everything, even the traffic jam and the frustration. Your line was this too is inside. Today, we live ashtpadi eleven. Day four hundred eighty-one.

Punjab is farming country, and a farmer there knows something in his bones that the rest of us learn slowly. You plow. You choose good seed. You sow it at the right time, straight and deep. You watch the canal, you pull the weeds, you get up before dawn for months. And then you wait for rain you cannot make, and sun you cannot order, and a harvest that is never entirely yours to decide. A lazy farmer has nothing to harvest. A farmer who thinks he controls the sky wears himself out. The good farmer does both: works, and lets go.
screen: `PLOW, SEED, SOW, WEED.` → `RAIN YOU CANNOT MAKE.` → `WORK, AND LET GO.`

segments.voice: Ashtpadi eleven has been saying, for three days, that God is the doer of all. Karan kaaran: the cause of causes. Jo tis bhaavai soee hog: whatever pleases Him comes to pass. Nothing outside the hukam. Heard on its own, that could sound like a reason to sit on the porch. Sikh teaching doesn't read it that way. The same Guru who wrote Sukhmani, Guru Arjan, wrote elsewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib a couplet on effort: make the effort, and live; earn, and enjoy peace; meditate, and meet God; Nanak, then anxiety is gone. The word for effort is udam: striving, enterprise, getting up and doing. So the Sikh picture has two hands. One hand works: udam, honest labor, what Sikhs call kirat karni, earning by your own effort. The other hand opens: bhaana, trust, leaving the outcome to the doer of all. Neither hand alone is the path. Effort without trust becomes anxiety, gripping the steering wheel of the whole road. Trust without effort becomes an excuse. Together, they give exactly what that couplet promises: anxiety is gone. Not because everything works out. Because you did your part fully, and you've stopped carrying the part that was never yours. That's how ashtpadi eleven is lived. Like the farmer: plow as if it all depends on you, then look at the sky as if it all depends on God.
screen: `THREE DAYS: GOD THE DOER.` · `UDAM: MAKE THE EFFORT.` · `ONE HAND WORKS, ONE HAND OPENS.` · `THEN ANXIETY IS GONE.` · then, large: `ACT, THEN RELEASE.`

segments.voice: The practice: act, then release. Pick one task in front of you today. Picture yourself doing it fully, properly, giving it real effort. See your hands busy. Now picture the moment it's done: the email sent, the meal served, the form submitted. Imagine opening your hands, palms up, like a farmer looking at the sky. Breathe in: I act. Breathe out: I release. Repeat it slowly, letting the two hands take turns. If you pray, you can offer the result to Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Udam, effort, striving. Trust and effort together: udam with one hand, bhaana with the other. Act, and leave the rest.
Your line: act, then release. Do one task today with your whole effort, and when it's done, open your hands and let the outcome go. Day four hundred eighty-one.

482.title: Ashtpadi 12, salok: the humble
482.howItsDone: In a gurdwara everyone sits on the floor at the same height, with only the Guru Granth Sahib raised, and in the langar people eat side by side in rows; Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib reach this salok at the opening of the twelfth ashtpadi.

segments.voice: Yesterday was living ashtpadi 11, udam, and your line: act, then release. Did you do one thing fully and then let the result go? Today Sukhmani opens a new ashtpadi, the twelfth. Day four hundred eighty-two.

Shoes come off at the door of a gurdwara. Heads are covered. And if you stay, you sit down on the floor. The hall is set up for sitting low: no pews, no front-row chairs, no reserved seats for donors. A surgeon sits beside a taxi driver. A grandmother sits beside a teenager who came straight from practice. One thing in the room is raised up: the Guru Granth Sahib, on its platform under a canopy. Everyone else is at the same height, and it's low. That floor is a lesson before anyone has said a word. Today the salok of the twelfth ashtpadi says it out loud.
screen: `SHOES OFF, HEAD COVERED.` → `EVERYONE SITS ON THE FLOOR.` → `ONLY THE GURU IS RAISED.`

segments.voice: The salok is two lines, and they lean against each other. The first says, in Guru Arjan's words, sukhee basai maskeeneeaa, aap nivaar tale. The meek one dwells in peace, having set the self down low. The second line is the mirror: the great, great proud ones, Nanak, are worn away by their own pride. Peace for the low, collapse for the high. The word for humility in Punjabi is nimrataa, and the salok's word, maskeen, is its close cousin: the meek one, the one who claims nothing. Notice the verb in the first line, though. Nivaar: to push aside, to remove. Humility here is not a feeling of being worthless. It's an action. You take the self, the loud, insisting part, and you set it down, the way you'd put down a heavy bag at the door. And the result is sukh, ease, the same sukh that sits in Sukhmani's own name. So this salok is close to the heart of the whole hymn. Why would lowering yourself bring ease? Look at what pride costs to keep up. It needs defending. It has to win the argument, get the credit, be seen at the right height. The proud person is always on guard duty. The humble one has put the guard down. Nobody can knock you off a seat you never climbed onto. The floor of the gurdwara and the rows of the langar, where people eat sitting side by side, can be read as this salok made physical. Nobody earns a higher place there. And the salok puts the peace exactly there: not in the words, but in the sitting down.
screen: `THE MEEK DWELL IN PEACE.` · `NIMRATAA: HUMILITY.` · `SET THE SELF DOWN, LIKE A BAG.` · `NO SEAT TO BE KNOCKED FROM.` · then, large: `THE HUMBLE REST EASY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take the lower seat, right now, in your body. If you can, sit on the floor for these two minutes. If you can't, simply lower your shoulders and let your chin drop a little. Then picture the self as a bag you've been carrying: your reputation, your need to be right. Set it down beside you. You can pick it up later. For now, just sit low, and notice whether anything gets easier. The bell holds the time.
Nimrataa. Humility: not thinking less of yourself, but setting the self down, low, the way the salok's meek one does. The salok promises that person peace.
Your line: the humble rest easy. Once today, take the lower seat on purpose: let someone else go first, sit at the back, or let a small point go unwon. Day four hundred eighty-two.

483.title: The proud fall
483.hook: the one who is proud of power will fall (Sukhmani 12)
483.howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib move through the stanzas of the twelfth ashtpadi, which name pride of power, beauty, wealth and good deeds, and Sikh teaching on seva prizes service done without show.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nimrataa, humility, and your line: the humble rest easy. Did you take a lower seat somewhere? It's the end of a week, and what a week: smaller worries, He is the doer, His will, this too is inside, act then release, and the humble at peace. Today, the other side of the coin. Day four hundred eighty-three.

There's a list Guru Arjan makes in the first stanza of the twelfth ashtpadi, and it reads like a lineup of the people the world envies. The one with power. The one who is young and good-looking. The one with money and land. You'd expect a hymn about pride to stop there. It doesn't. Slipped into the same list, right next to the rich and the beautiful, is someone who seems to belong on the other team entirely: the person who is proud of being good. Today: the proud fall, and the surprise of who counts as proud.
screen: `POWER. YOUTH. MONEY AND LAND.` → `AND ONE MORE NAME ON THE LIST.` → `THE ONE PROUD OF BEING GOOD.`

segments.voice: Yesterday's salok said the great, proud ones are worn away by their own pride. Now the stanzas show us what that pride looks like. Each line names one kind, and each kind gets a blunt picture of where it ends. Whoever carries the pride of ruling inside, the text says, sinks as low as a dog. Whoever thinks, I am young and beautiful, ends up as a worm in filth. The images are harsh on purpose. Guru Arjan isn't being polite about something he thinks is dangerous. And then the turn, before the stanza even reaches wealth. Whoever calls himself a doer of good deeds, the stanza says, wanders through birth after birth. Only then comes wealth: whoever is proud of money and land, he calls a blind, ignorant fool. The good-deeds line is the one that stops a reader. The Guru Granth Sahib praises good deeds, and Sikh life is full of them: serving in the langar, giving to people in need, standing up for the weak. So what's wrong with doing good? Nothing. What the stanza warns about is the calling yourself. Good done and then worn like a medal turns into the same thing as the crown and the bank account: something to stand on, something to be seen with. The salok's word for the proud was ahankaaree, from ahankaar, ego, the voice that says: I did this. The pride is the same in all four, and so is the fall. The salok already said how: the proud are worn away by their own pride. Pride needs height. Height means a drop. The bigger the pedestal, the farther down the floor.
screen: `POWER AND YOUTH: EACH FALLS.` · `BLUNT PICTURES, ON PURPOSE.` · `EVEN PRIDE IN GOOD DEEDS.` · `AHANKAAR: THE VOICE THAT SAYS I.` · then, large: `PRIDE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: catch one proud thought. Sit quietly and let the mind run. Sooner or later it will bring up something like, I handled that well, or I'm not like those people, or at least I'm the one who helps. When it does, don't scold it. Just notice it, the way you'd notice a car going by, and name it softly: pride. Then let it pass and wait for the next one. Even catching one is the practice. The bell holds the time.
Ahankaar, pride, ego. Pride of power, of youth, of wealth, and even of good deeds: the voice that says I did this, and every pedestal has a drop.
Your line: pride falls. Today, if you catch yourself telling a story where you come off well, try telling it without that part. Day four hundred eighty-three.

options: in volunteering too much.
in wearing the good deed like a medal.

fork.reveal: the stanza names whoever calls himself a doer of good deeds. the good is fine; the calling yourself is the pedestal.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ahankaar, pride, ego; the sense of making a me.

trapdoor: what you thought: pride is a rich person's problem.
what it means: pride is anything you stand on to be higher, even your own goodness.
what a scholar hears: ahankaar comes from Sanskrit ahamkara, aham, I, plus kara, making; Sikh teaching counts it among the five thieves.
